rewrite: A shorter, more rock-radio-leaning record made as the band toured constantly and the personal frictions that would soon push Isbell out started to show. It trades some concept-album ambition for tighter, punchier songs like 'Space City' and 'Aftermath USA', though the storytelling instincts stay intact. It shows a band stretching toward a more straightforward rock sound, for listeners who want DBT at its most direct.

problems: Jay Gonzalez was already in the band, not newly settling in
rewrite: The first album after a three-year studio gap and a lineup shake-up, with Shonna Tucker and John Neff gone and bassist Matt Patton newly aboard, and a return to an even split of Hood and Cooley songs after Cooley had contributed fewer songs for years. Cooley's 'Made Up English Oceans' and 'Primer Coat' are among his sharpest character studies, while Hood's songs turn toward middle-aged reflection. It reasserts the band's two-songwriter-plus-guitars core after a decade of expanding lineups.

problems: 'widely treated as most urgent' critic claim
influence on Lee Bains III/American Aquarium unsupported (Lee Bains predates it)
rewrite: An overtly political record made in the year of the 2016 election, tackling police shootings, gun culture and the Confederate flag head-on in songs like Hood's 'What It Means' and Cooley's 'Ramon Casiano'. It trades some of the earlier albums' novelistic distance for direct address, restating the band's long-held position that Southern pride and white supremacy are not the same thing. It is the place to start for listeners who want the band at its most urgent and topical.

Written in response to family separations at the border, mass shootings and the Trump years, this is the angriest and most direct record in the catalog, with Hood's 'Thoughts and Prayers' and 'Babies in Cages' naming their targets outright. Hood writes the bulk of the record, with Cooley contributing only a little. It is more topical broadside than character study, a departure from the band's usual novelistic method.

A surprise album released months after The Unraveling, mixing leftover songs from those sessions with new material written during the COVID-19 lockdown and the protests of summer 2020, including the unrest-themed title track. It is looser and more urgent-sounding than a normal studio album, closer to a dispatch from a specific summer than a planned statement. Hood's voice dominates, and the guitars are rough and immediate.

problems: Club XIII dates to Hood and Cooley's 1980s pre-DBT days, not the band's 1990s beginnings
rewrite: A loose, funny, nostalgic record looking back at Hood and Cooley's scrappy beginnings playing a Muscle Shoals-area club in their teens and twenties, a deliberate return to warmth and humor after two angry, topical albums. Cooley's 'Every Single Storied Flameout' looks at the touring life, while Hood's title track recalls those earliest gigs by name. It brings back the bar-band energy of the early records decades on, for fans who miss the band's sense of humor.

problems: serial-killer song and session-family-history song claims unverified
piano and 'sketchbook for later band songs' claims unverified
rewrite: Hood's first solo album is a stark, largely acoustic set of songs that did not fit Drive-By Truckers, recorded quickly and cheaply. It is quieter and more intimate than any DBT record, foregrounding Hood's plainspoken, conversational voice over sparse guitar on songs like the title track and 'Belinda Carlisle Diet'. It plays like a demo-like sketchbook, for fans who want the storyteller without the three-guitar wall.

problems: recording date/shelving story wrong: the album was cut around 2008 with DBT members, not in 2001
lineage tied to wrong pre-SRO period
rewrite: Collecting songs Hood had written over many years, some dating back well before Drive-By Truckers took off, Murdering Oscar is a full-band record rather than a solo sketchbook. It sounds closer to a DBT side project than the stripped-down Killers and Stars, with loud guitars and harmony vocals dressing up songs about doomed romance and Southern family history. It is for fans who want more of Hood's dark, funny storytelling in a rowdier setting.

problems: Hood moved to Portland later (c. 2015), not before this album
rewrite: A more atmospheric, reflective solo record with a fuller, more layered band sound than Hood's earlier solo work. Songs like '12:01' and 'Come Back Little Star' deal with aging, loss and looking back, sung in his plainspoken narrative voice over slow-burning guitars. It is for listeners who like Hood's writing but want it quieter and more inward than a Truckers record.

problems: two-disc format and new/old-material mix unverified
rewrite: Hood's most recent solo album continues the plainspoken, personal storytelling of his earlier solo work while looking back on family, age and memory. It keeps the same core method as his prior solo records: narrative verses delivered in his conversational drawl over a full-band arrangement. As his fourth solo album in two decades, it confirms Hood treats his solo work as a slower-moving, more reflective counterpart to Drive-By Truckers.

A solo acoustic live album stripping Drive-By Truckers songs like 'Zip City' and 'Marry Me' down to just Cooley's voice, guitar and dry between-song banter. It highlights Cooley's plainer, funnier, more deadpan songwriting style, since there is no full band arrangement to fill in the space. It is a rare chance to hear the other half of DBT's two-songwriter partnership on his own.

problems: divorce/drinking framing of 'Try' and 'Dress Blues' unsupported; 'Dress Blues' is about a Marine killed in Iraq
rewrite: Isbell's solo debut, written largely during his last years in Drive-By Truckers and released shortly after his 2007 departure from the band, with Patterson Hood and other DBT members guesting on several tracks. Songs like 'Try' and 'Dress Blues', about a young Marine from his hometown killed in Iraq, show the same novelistic character-writing he brought to Decoration Day and The Dirty South, now in a warmer, more personal register. It is the clear hinge between his Truckers years and the solo career that found its own lane with Southeastern.

problems: 'last album before polished shift' wrong (Here We Rest followed)
rewrite: Isbell's second solo album and the first billed to his new backing band the 400 Unit, made as he settled into life after Drive-By Truckers, with songs like 'Cigarettes and Wine' circling drinking and regret. It keeps the story-song DNA of his Truckers work but with a tight, rock-oriented band of guitars and keyboards behind him. It is for listeners who want Isbell's writing with Southern-rock muscle rather than the quieter polish of his later records.

problems: lineage is scene resemblance, not documented
rewrite: Lucero's self-titled debut is a raw, road-worn blend of punk energy and country heartbreak from a Memphis band. Ben Nichols' cracked, whiskey-worn voice carries songs about broke-down luck and drinking through heartbreak, closer in spirit to the Replacements than to polished Nashville country. It set the template the band refined over the next two decades: unpretentious, guitar-driven story-songs built for a bar full of people who already know the words.

Lucero's second album leans further into countryish twang without losing the band's punk backbone, on a record about leaving and coming back to the South. Nichols writes about touring exhaustion and romantic failure in short, direct verses rather than elaborate narrative, closer to a diary than a short story. It shows the band tightening its songwriting while keeping the bar-band grit of the debut.

problems: 'written and recorded during near-constant touring' unverified method claim
rewrite: A road album in subject and feel, with songs about the exhaustion and loneliness of life on the highway between shows. It keeps the same scratchy, live-sounding production as the first two records, favoring a full-band, played-live feel over studio polish. Restlessness is the record's throughline, matching a band still building its audience one club date at a time.

problems: 'most often cited by later bands' lineage unsupported
rewrite: The record where Lucero's songwriting got sharper without losing its bar-band heart, built around Nichols' cracked, conversational delivery on songs like the title track and 'Sweet Little Thing'. The band starts to sound like a unit rather than a frontman-plus-backing-band, with tighter arrangements and more melodic hooks than the earlier, rougher records. It is where the band's mix of punk toughness and country heartbreak fully clicks, a good first stop for new listeners.

problems: title is not the address of the studio where it was cut
rewrite: Named for a Memphis address tied to the band's history, this is the first Lucero album to add a horn section, pushing the band's sound toward the Memphis soul and Stax tradition alongside its punk and country roots. It is a fuller, more ambitious production than the band's earlier records, without losing Nichols' plainspoken storytelling. It is for listeners who want their bar-band heartbreak with brass and organ behind it.

problems: 'horns permanent' claim contradicted by later records
rewrite: A horn-driven, barroom-ready record made after the band signed to ATO, with 'Downtown' capturing the album's mix of bar-band swagger and Memphis soul horns. It is one of Lucero's most purely fun records, built for dancing as much as listening, while still carrying Nichols' plainspoken songwriting about work, love and getting by. It is the pick for listeners who want the band at its loosest and loudest.

A darker, more atmospheric record, with keyboardist Rick Steff's piano and organ pushed further into the arrangements than on the horn-heavy Women & Work. Nichols' songwriting turns toward distance, family and mortality on tracks like 'Went Looking for Warren Zevon's Los Angeles', trading barroom energy for a heavier, more reflective mood. It shows a band twenty years in still finding new emotional territory rather than repeating itself.

problems: Centro-matic is not a cowpunk act; DBT parallel is resemblance

rewrite: A louder, more confident follow-up that tightened the band's songwriting while keeping its beer-soaked live energy, with Brent Best's character songs about restless small-town life sharpening into something closer to short fiction. The interplay between rhythm and lead guitars gives the record a rougher, more garage-rock edge than most of the alt-country bands it got lumped in with. It is for listeners who like their twang loud and a little sloppy.

problems: American Aquarium/Two Cow influence claims unsupported
rewrite: This is where Brent Best's songwriting fully matches the band's live intensity, with 'Josephine' standing as one of the band's best-loved songs. It balances big, distorted guitar choruses with plainspoken verses about failed relationships and small-town dead ends. The New West deal gave the record wider distribution than the band's earlier Doolittle releases, and it is the natural starting point for new listeners.

problems: band-member and Budapest One details unverified
rewrite: The album from the Drams, the band Slobberbone frontman Brent Best formed after Slobberbone's initial breakup. It keeps Best's plainspoken storytelling but leans toward a slightly more melodic, harmonized-guitar sound than Slobberbone's rawer records. It stands as a bridge between Slobberbone's original run and its later reunion, for fans who want Best's songs with a little more polish.

problems: shared touring circuit with Lucero/the Drams unsupported
DIY-circuit ties to Glossary/the Drams unsupported
rewrite: A rowdier, more explicitly punk-leaning record made as the band's touring schedule intensified, with Micah Schnabel's songwriting turning more self-critical. The interplay between Schnabel and co-frontman Shane Sweeney gives the record two distinct, contrasting narrative voices within the same hard-driving arrangements. It is for listeners who like their alt-country loud, fast and bruised.

problems: Shane Sweeney did not leave the band (still present on later records)
rewrite: This record finds Micah Schnabel leaning further into plainspoken, autobiographical storytelling, with Shane Sweeney still supplying a contrasting second voice. It trades some of the earlier records' raw shouting for a slightly more measured, road-worn delivery, though the guitar-forward arrangements stay simple and direct. It marks a turning point toward the more reflective songwriting of the band's later records.

problems: songwriter attribution of 'Let the Boys Be Girls' unverified
John Moreland/Adam Faucett labelmate link partly unverified
rewrite: A more explicitly political record made in a divided America, with the inclusive anthem 'Let the Boys Be Girls' standing as one of the band's most direct statements after years of mostly personal songwriting. It keeps the band's simple, road-tested guitar-bass-drums attack while aiming its storytelling outward at the country's politics rather than inward at touring life. It shows a band well into its run still finding new subjects to write about.

problems: band-member names (Smith) and Glorietta/Deslondes claims unverified
rewrite: A bigger, more anthemic record than Glossary's earlier, scrappier albums, with choruses built for rooms rather than bars. The songs keep circling small-town Tennessee subjects, faith and hard luck, sung in a plainspoken voice over twin guitars and a warm rhythm section. It is for listeners who want Southern storytelling rock with big-hearted, sing-along hooks.

problems: Barham citing Isbell as model unsupported; Isbell produced the album
rewrite: BJ Barham's band cut this after years of van-touring poverty, and it plays like a document of that grind: plainspoken songs about broke bank accounts, failed relationships and the toll of chasing a music career on the road. Barham's voice is more conversational than powerful, closer to a bar-stool confession than a performance, which suits the record's unglamorous subject matter. It is where American Aquarium's songwriting caught up to its Drive-By Truckers- and Lucero-indebted sound.

problems: lineup breakup came after this album, not before
title-track subject and 'generally treated' claims unsupported
rewrite: A harder, more self-examining record about the wreckage of the touring years documented on Burn. Flicker. Die., with Barham looking squarely at drinking, distance and what the road costs the people at home. It keeps the band's plainspoken, roadhouse sound, big guitars and steel behind a conversational vocal. It is for listeners who want the hangover after the party records.

A fuller-sounding, more explicitly political record made after Barham became a father, turning some of the band's usual drinking-and-heartbreak subject matter toward the state of the country and what he wants to pass on to his daughter. 'A Better South' keeps the plainspoken, conversational vocal delivery of the earlier records but wraps it in a bigger, more polished New West production. It is for listeners who want Southern storytelling rock that argues with its own region.

A genre-hopping record that moves between punk-speed rockers, aching piano ballads and pure country weepers within the same album, matching the title's mixed-breed idea to Branan's restless songwriting. It is less a single-mood record than a demonstration of range, tied together by Branan's dense, wordplay-heavy lyrics and Memphis-honed storytelling instincts. It is the best single sampler of everything he can do.

A tighter, more focused follow-up to Mutt's genre sprawl, built around Branan's talking, self-deprecating songs about failed ambition and the compromises of a working songwriter's life, as on 'Survivor Blues'. It keeps the same dense wordplay and dark humor as his earlier records while sounding more like a full-band rock record than a singer-songwriter set. It is for listeners who want funny-sad lyrics with a bar band's push behind them.

problems: shared labels/stages claim unsupported; the concrete link is Lee Bains III's membership
rewrite: A Tuscaloosa, Alabama band's garage-rock-scaled take on Southern storytelling rock, cut louder and grungier than the more polished Muscle Shoals end of the scene, with slide guitar and fuzzed-out riffs driving songs about hard-luck small-town Alabama life. It sits closer to garage-blues than to Drive-By Truckers' novelistic three-guitar sound, but the small-town, unglamorous subject matter is the same. It is for listeners who want their Southern rock sweaty and loud.

A more focused follow-up to Young Criminals' Starvation League, trading some of that record's eccentric sprawl for a tighter set of songs about romantic wreckage. Bare Jr.'s deadpan, half-spoken delivery keeps the record from tipping into straightforward heartbreak balladry, undercutting its own sadness with dry jokes. It continues his run of Nashville-outsider storytelling rock on Bloodshot Records.

An Austin record that marked the band's shift away from straight alt-country toward louder, more distorted guitar rock. Twin-guitar interplay carries plainspoken songs about drinking and hard luck, closer to a Texas take on Drive-By Truckers' harmonized-guitar approach than to the twangier Austin singer-songwriter scene around them. It represents the moment the band found its own version of Southern storytelling rock.

problems: 'merger of earlier Mississippi and Arkansas projects' unverified
'faith and doubt at near-whisper' and 'most slowcore' claims unverified
rewrite: The self-titled third album keeps Kinkel-Schuster and Bryant's songs slow, unresolved and plainly worded, with close harmonies and unhurried arrangements that leave plenty of air around the voices. The faint twang of the earlier records is still there, but the mood is heavier and more inward. It is for listeners who like Southern songwriting at a hush rather than a holler.

problems: Prine link better grounded in Oh Boy label; Hood link is resemblance
rewrite: A loose, talky record made after Snider settled into the scrappier East Nashville side of town, mixing plainspoken story-songs with dry, self-deprecating humor. 'Play a Train Song', written for a friend who died young, shows Snider's ability to turn a joke into grief within the same verse, the same funny-sad method John Prine made his own. It is the best place to hear his deadpan, talking-blues style at full strength.

A slightly bigger-sounding, more electric record than East Nashville Skyline, turning Snider's talking-blues storytelling toward more overtly political targets in mid-2000s America. It keeps the same deadpan, conversational delivery as his other records, using humor as a way into serious subjects rather than avoiding them, as on 'Tension'. It shows Snider expanding his East Nashville persona into a wider social-commentary role.

problems: theme misdescribed (record centers on class and money more than mortality)
rewrite: Released on Snider's own Aimless Records, this record turns his talking-blues storytelling toward money, class and religion without losing the dry humor of his earlier work. Songs like 'Precious Little Miracles' keep the funny-sad balance of grief and jokes in the same verse that defines his whole catalog. It shows a songwriter in his mid-40s using the same plainspoken method to take on bigger questions.

problems: DBT is not an Oklahoma band
rewrite: Moreland's solo album trades his earlier punk-band background for plainspoken acoustic songs carried by his weathered baritone, with 'Nobody Gives a Damn About Songwriters Anymore' laying out his wry, self-aware view of the trade. It shares the unglamorous, working-class subject matter of Southern storytelling rock, but set in Oklahoma and delivered mostly solo rather than through a three-guitar band. It is for listeners who want the most direct, emotionally exposed version of this lane.

problems: In the Throes was not his debut
'best-known song' claim and placement of 'Break My Heart Sweetly' uncertain (may be from In the Throes)
rewrite: A fuller-band, more melodic follow-up to In the Throes, showcasing Moreland's ability to write devastating lines in plain, unadorned language on songs like 'Hang Me in the Tulsa County Stars'. It keeps the same weathered baritone and Oklahoma small-town subject matter as his earlier records, but with more developed arrangements of organ, electric guitar and drums behind it. It is the natural starting point for anyone new to him.

A more atmospheric, textured record, adding subtle synths, drum machines and studio effects to Moreland's baritone and acoustic guitar in a way that departs from the straightforward full-band sound of Big Bad Luv. Tracks like 'Terrestrial' lean into hazier, more processed textures, while the plainspoken, self-questioning songwriting stays intact. It shows Moreland deliberately complicating his own singer-songwriter formula rather than repeating it.

Continuing the more textured direction of LP5, this record keeps Moreland's plainspoken baritone at the center while layering in subtle electronic touches around the acoustic core. It is a quieter, more interior record than his mid-2010s full-band albums, closer to a home-recorded diary than a road-band statement. It confirms the more atmospheric turn Moreland took after Big Bad Luv rather than a return to his earlier straightforward Americana sound.

problems: nonsensical 'first English-language recording of a Dylan song sung in French' claim
rewrite: Released only months before Liege & Lief, Unhalfbricking is the transitional record where Fairport worked out how electric folk-rock should sound: three Bob Dylan covers, including the French-language 'Si Tu Dois Partir', sit next to Sandy Denny's own 'Who Knows Where the Time Goes?'. Dave Swarbrick's guest fiddle on the long traditional 'A Sailor's Life' pushed the band into the modal, drone-heavy sound that became their signature. Drummer Martin Lamble died in the van crash that followed the album's sessions, closing the band's first era.

problems: 'Down in the Flood' is a Bob Dylan song, not 'Brenda's'
rewrite: Sandy Denny's debut solo album after leaving Fotheringay pairs her own increasingly personal songwriting, especially the elegiac 'Late November' and the war-haunted 'John the Gun', with Bob Dylan's 'Down in the Flood' and the traditional 'Blackwaterside'. Her old Fairport bandmates and members of Fotheringay back her, so the sound stays close to electric folk-rock even as the album is billed as a solo statement. It set the pattern for her run of solo records through the mid-1970s.

problems: no Cliff Richard duet: 'Whispering Grass' is a solo cover
rewrite: Denny's third solo album pushes further into orchestrated pop and cabaret, with her cover of the old standard 'Whispering Grass' sitting alongside the stark 'At the End of the Day' and 'No End', one of the bleakest things she recorded. Her piano and strings take the lead more often than guitars, and her voice is at its most burnished. It is less often discussed than her Fairport-era work but shows her range past straight folk-rock.

problems: not his first album after Fairport (Henry the Human Fly came first)
rewrite: The first Richard and Linda Thompson album, with Linda singing lead on several tracks, is bleaker and more electric than anything in the Fairport catalog: 'The Calvary Cross' and 'Withered and Died' pair Richard's angular guitar lines with grim, plainspoken lyrics. Linda Thompson's voice, clear and slightly weary, gives the songs a different weight than Sandy Denny's Fairport-era singing. It set the template for the duo's run of albums together.

problems: 'sparer, not full band' claim wrong (band backing present)
lineage wrongly implies no albums between this and Shoot Out the Lights
rewrite: Recorded soon after the Thompsons converted to Sufi Islam, Pour Down Like Silver trades Hokey Pokey's music-hall jokes for devotional, often severe songs like 'Night Comes In' and 'For Shame of Doing Wrong'. Richard Thompson's guitar takes long, searching solos over a steady folk-rock band while Linda's voice stays grave and controlled. It closes out the pair's mid-1970s run before a gap in their recording career.

Produced by Joe Boyd and made as the Thompsons' marriage was ending, Shoot Out the Lights is a harder, more rock-oriented record than their earlier albums, with Richard Thompson's guitar solos on 'Walking on a Wire' and the title track carrying real menace. Linda Thompson's vocals on songs about failing love add a tension that is hard to hear past. It was their last studio record together, and the one to start with.

problems: 'River Man' strings were arranged by Harry Robinson, not Robert Kirby
rewrite: Nick Drake's debut, produced by Joe Boyd and arranged largely by Robert Kirby, sets his hushed, intricately fingerpicked guitar and low, unhurried voice against chamber strings on songs like 'River Man' and 'Way to Blue'. It sold poorly on release but has since become a touchstone of quiet British songwriting. The playing is technically demanding but never shows off; the mood stays melancholy and controlled throughout.

problems: wording implied Fairport members played on 'Northern Sky' (Cale is the guest there)
rewrite: Drake's second album adds horns, congas and members of Fairport Convention, with John Cale guesting on 'Northern Sky', pushing his sound toward a breezier, almost jazz-folk pop arrangement without losing the close, intimate guitar work underneath. 'At the Chime of a City Clock' and the instrumental title track show Robert Kirby's arrangements working with the songs rather than around them. It remains the outlier in Drake's catalog, warmer and more outward-facing than Five Leaves Left or Pink Moon.

Recorded in two late-night sessions with just Drake's voice, guitar and a single piano overdub on the title track, Pink Moon strips away the string arrangements of his first two albums entirely. It is his shortest and starkest record, under half an hour long, made as his depression deepened; he died two years later. It is for listeners who want acoustic songwriting at its most unadorned and intimate.

problems: kitchen/flat-fee recording details trimmed as unverifiable
lineage claims about Nick Drake and American Primitive unsupported
rewrite: Recorded cheaply on a borrowed tape machine, Bert Jansch's debut announced a new, harder-edged British fingerstyle guitar sound built from folk, blues and jazz phrasing. 'Needle of Death', a plainspoken song about a friend's heroin overdose, and 'Angie', his version of Davy Graham's instrumental, became touchstones for guitarists including Jimmy Page and Neil Young. The recording is rough and close-miked, which only adds to its intensity.

problems: Pentangle was a five-piece, not a duo (the duo was Bert and John)

rewrite: Made in Los Angeles with former Monkee Michael Nesmith producing, L.A. Turnaround pairs Jansch's fingerstyle guitar with American session players for a sound noticeably warmer and more country-inflected than his Transatlantic-era records, including a re-recorded 'Needle of Death' and the loping 'Fresh as a Sweet Sunday Morning'. Pedal steel and easy, rolling rhythms soften his usually austere playing. The Nesmith connection ties the British folk guitar tradition directly to the Los Angeles country-rock scene.

problems: Echoplex showcase is 'Glistening Glyndebourne', not 'Head and Heart'
rewrite: Bless the Weather is the record where John Martyn's acoustic guitar started taking on the tape-echo and Echoplex treatments that would define his later work, most clearly on the instrumental 'Glistening Glyndebourne'. Danny Thompson's double bass gives songs like 'Head and Heart' and the title track a loose, jazz-inflected pulse under Martyn's slurred, soulful phrasing. It sits right at the point where British folk guitar starts bending toward jazz and dub.

problems: Echoplex showcase is 'I'd Rather Be the Devil', not 'Don't Want to Know'
rewrite: Solid Air is John Martyn's best-known record, built around the title track, a slow, vibraphone-tinged song written for his friend Nick Drake. 'May You Never' is his most familiar song, 'Don't Want to Know' is a warm, hopeful ballad, and 'I'd Rather Be the Devil' shows off the Echoplex-treated guitar sound he had been developing since Bless the Weather. Danny Thompson's double bass and a loose, jazz-club atmosphere separate it from the harder-edged folk-rock of Fairport or Steeleye Span.

Pentangle's third album is where the group's fusion of folk song, jazz interplay and blues fully clicked, led by 'Light Flight', which was used as the theme to the TV series Take Three Girls. Bert Jansch and John Renbourn's interlocking guitars, Jacqui McShee's clear soprano and the jazz rhythm section of Danny Thompson and Terry Cox give traditional songs like 'Once I Had a Sweetheart' a loose, swinging feel closer to a jazz combo than a folk group. It is the best single introduction to the band.

Unlike Briggs's earlier unaccompanied traditional-song recordings, The Time Has Come turns to contemporary songs, several of her own, sung over her own acoustic guitar and, on one track, Johnny Moynihan's bouzouki. Her plain, unornamented voice and the sparse arrangements make songs like the title track and 'Wishing Well' feel closer to a field recording than a produced folk-rock album. It is for listeners who want British folk at its barest and most private.

problems: 'Blue Monk' is Thelonious Monk's tune, not Graham's own
rewrite: A collaboration between traditional-song singer Shirley Collins and guitar innovator Davy Graham, this album set English and American folk songs like 'Nottamun Town' and 'Reynardine' against Graham's blues- and jazz-inflected fingerstyle guitar, including an instrumental take on Thelonious Monk's 'Blue Monk'. Graham's open-tuning, modal approach to the guitar became foundational for the British fingerstyle players who followed him. It predates the main folk-rock era by a few years but already sounds like British folk guitar going modern.

Vashti Bunyan wrote these songs on a real horse-and-wagon journey from London toward Donovan's planned commune on Skye; Joe Boyd produced the finished record with Robert Kirby's gentle string arrangements and guest musicians from Fairport Convention and the Incredible String Band. It sold almost nothing on release and Bunyan left music for three decades. The album's hushed, lullaby-like songs about the journey, especially 'Diamond Day' and 'Rose Hip November', were rediscovered around 2000 and became a touchstone for the freak-folk and indie-folk revivals.

Steeleye Span's second album, made by the band Ashley Hutchings formed after leaving Fairport Convention, is harder and starker than Fairport's records: there is no drummer, and Maddy Prior and Martin Carthy's voices carry songs like 'The Blacksmith' and 'False Knight on the Road' over interlocking electric guitars. It is one of the most purely traditional of the classic British electric-folk albums, less rock-band than Liege & Lief. The band would soften toward pop with Below the Salt and later hits.

problems: UK chart position and Peel-championing claims unsupported
rewrite: Chapman's second album, cut with a pre-fame Mick Ronson on lead guitar and Rick Kemp (later of Steeleye Span) on bass, is built around his best-known song, 'Postcards of Scarborough', a plainspoken portrait of a fading English seaside town. His guitar playing draws on the same fingerstyle vocabulary as Bert Jansch and Davy Graham, but his gravelly, conversational voice and travelogue lyrics push the songs closer to folk-rock storytelling than pure guitar showcase. It is for listeners who want British folk guitar with road dust and electric bite.

problems: 'Less Than You Think' is not the closing track ('The Late Greats' closes)
rewrite: Tweedy played almost all the lead guitar himself here, stretching into krautrock-length jams on 'Spiders (Kidsmoke)' and sinking into the long drone-and-feedback coda of 'Less Than You Think', made as he struggled with migraines and painkiller addiction. It is Wilco's most abrasive record, trading the studio collage of 'Yankee Hotel Foxtrot' for raw, extended guitar playing. Nels Cline would join the band soon after and stay for good.

A double live album recorded over four nights at Chicago's Vic Theatre, capturing the new lineup with Nels Cline and Pat Sansone and stretching the 'Yankee Hotel Foxtrot' and 'A Ghost Is Born' catalog into longer, more guitar-forward arrangements. It is the best document of how strong the post-2004 six-piece lineup was live, for anyone who wants the noise and the tunes at once.

problems: 'Art of Almost' is about seven minutes; the twelve-minute track is closer 'One Sunday Morning'
rewrite: The first release on Wilco's own dBpm imprint reintroduced some of the studio adventurousness of the early 2000s, opening with the seven-minute art-rock collage 'Art of Almost' and closing with the gentle twelve-minute acoustic ballad 'One Sunday Morning'. It sits between the noise records and the classic-rock records, pulling from both, with 'I Might' as its bright pop center.

Surprise-released for free with a cat-painting cover and no advance notice, this is Wilco's shortest, loosest, most garage-rock record, all fuzzed-out guitars and songs that end almost as soon as they start. It feels far from the polish of 'Wilco (The Album)', for listeners who like the band scrappy and loud.

problems: Tweedy's solo records came after, so it cannot share sessions with them

rewrite: A warmer, more song-based second Loose Fur record, arriving as Wilco itself was settling into the guitar-forward sound of 'Sky Blue Sky', with Tweedy, O'Rourke and Kotche trading the first album's studio abstraction for straighter tunes. Songs like 'Hey Chicago' sound like a relaxed, slightly wry Wilco side session.

A fuller-band, more orchestrated record than the debut, adding strings and horns to Will Sheff's storytelling on songs like 'Song of Our So-Called Friend' and pointing toward the more ambitious 'Black Sheep Boy'. River imagery and wounded, literate narrators run through the whole set. It is for listeners who like folk-rock with a novelist's eye and a chamber band's colors.

problems: 'widely considered masterpiece' and 'put scene on the map' claims unsupported
rewrite: Built around Tim Hardin's 1960s song of the same name, this concept record follows the fictional 'Black Sheep Boy' through addiction and heartbreak, with Will Sheff's voice cracking between hushed verses and full-band eruptions. Songs like 'For Real' swing from whisper to roar, while 'A King and a Queen' is tender and spare. It is the essential Okkervil River record.

problems: John Berryman did not drown (he jumped from a bridge)
rewrite: A record about performance and fame, opening with the driving 'Our Life Is Not a Movie or Maybe' and threading references to a dead porn actress and a poet's suicide through Sheff's most anthemic songwriting yet. It is the record where the band's sound became fuller and more rock-oriented without losing the literary density.
